newsitem.title: ITALY: Indicted Berlusconi aide slams Italy "inquisition".
newsitem.headline: Indicted Berlusconi aide slams Italy "inquisition".

text.p: A former key aide to centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi slammed Italian magistrates as "Nazis" and "inquisitors" on Wednesday after they sought to have him put on trial on charges of collaborating with the Mafia.

Their 500-page indictment alleged that Marcello Dell'Utri, ex-boss of former prime minister Berlusconi's Publitalia advertising company, had acted as a go-between for the mafia and businessmen in Milan since the mid-1970s.

The allegations marked the latest battle in the centre-right's ongoing war with the magistrature and newspapers said it was a blow for Forza Italia, which Dell'Utri helped Berlusconi to found and bring to power in 1994.

Berlusconi's government, sensationally elected after the ruling old guard collapsed in a string of corruption scandals and allegations of collusion with Cosa Nostra, was short-lived and collapsed after just seven stormy months.
Dell'Utri, himself a Sicilian and a deputy for Forza Italia, dismissed the magistrates' claims as "lies," "balls" and a cooked-up plot designed to inflict maximum political damage.

"The case against Berlusconi and me was opened at the end of 1993 when we were both planning to launch into politics with Forza Italia and present ourselves in the (1994) elections," he told the daily La Repubblica newspaper.
"The coincidence in timing makes me suspicious."
Dell'Utri denounced the evidence of 17 Mafia turncoats contained in the indictment, saying prosecutors relied on the evidence of "common delinquents, assassins, professional liars."
"To make everything up to discredit a person is a method inaugurated by Goebbels," he told La Stampa, referring to Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.
"(The investigating magistrates) are not judges, they are inquisitors...I thought they were normal people, men who were after the truth."

Both Dell'Utri and Berlusconi are already on trial in separate cases of alleged corruption. Both deny wrongdoing but Dell'Utri resigned as Publitalia chairman last year when charges of false billing and tax fraud at the company emerged.
Media mogul Berlusconi has already accused the judiciary of waging a Stalinist plot to destroy his political career.
The preliminary hearing to decide whether to send Dell'Utri to trial for criminal association with the Mafia is scheduled to start on November 22 in the Sicilian capital Palermo.

Newspapers quoted the head of Palermo's public prosecutors office, Giancarlo Caselli, as saying that Dell'Utri maintained links with a string of Mafia figures, including the Mob's boss of bosses Salvatore Riina, who is now in jail.
According to the prosecution, Dell'Utri laundered millions of dollars of dirty money from the Naples mafia, the Camorra, with the help of the Sicilian Mafia.
Much of Sicily voted for Forza Italia in the 1994 general election and opponents have accused the Mafia of backing it.
"So I've been Cosa Nostra's man in northern Italy? OK. From 1970 to 1995? Wrong," Dell'Utri told La Stampa.
"I must still be then. Why would I resign...(from Publitalia) but not from Cosa Nostra? It would have been rude to leave them with no reference in the north, don't you think."
